title: The window in the old palace
translation: When the present palace was built, the experts on court customs went over it and found nothing wrong anywhere. The emperor was about to move in when his grandmother, Genki Mon'in, took one look and said: "In the old Kan'in palace, the comb-shaped window was round, with no frame." That palace had burned down decades before. Impressive.
Sure enough, the new window had notches cut into it and a wooden frame, so it was wrong, and they fixed it.
original: {今|いま}の{内裏|だいり}つくりいだされて、{有職|いうそく}の{人々|ひとびと}に{見|み}せられけるに、いづくも{難|なん}なしとて、すでに{遷幸|せんかう}の{日|ひ}{近|ちか}くなりけるに、{玄輝門院|げんきもんゐん}{御覧|ごらん}じて、「{閑院殿|かんゐんどの}の{櫛形|くしがた}の{穴|あな}は、まろく{縁|ふち}もなくてぞありし。」と{仰|おほ}せられける、いみじかりけり。
これは{葉|えふ}の{入|い}りて、{木|き}にて{縁|ふち}をしたりければ、{誤|あやま}りにて{直|なほ}されにけり。
literal: When the present palace had been built and was shown to people versed in court precedent, they said there was no flaw anywhere, and when the day of the emperor's move was already near, the Genki Mon'in looked at it and said, 'At the Kan'in palace, the comb-shaped opening was round and had no frame': that was splendid.
This (new one) had notches and was framed with wood, so it was a mistake and was corrected.

notes.text: Tōin Inshi (1246–1329), the mother of Emperor Fushimi and grandmother of Emperor Hanazono, for whom the new palace was built (1317). She had known the old Kan'in palace and remembered how it looked.

The Kan'in palace served as the main imperial residence until it burned in 1259, almost sixty years before the new palace (probably 1317). The 'comb-shaped opening' was a half-round window in the wall of the emperor's quarters, shaped like the top of a comb.
{葉|えふ}: probably notched or leaf-shaped edges cut into the opening. Commentators are not certain of the exact detail. The point is clear anyway: the experts missed it, and she remembered.
'That was splendid.' Kenkō admires exact memory of old forms (compare section 22).
